title: Agent Memory Distillation: Empowering Small LLM Agents with Hierarchical Teacher Memory

visual_explainer.blocker: Two isolated GPT Image attempts on 2026-08-12 ignored the paper-specific AMD brief and rendered an unrelated Agent Memory Radar dashboard with fabricated papers, counts, dates, and repository status instead of the hierarchical teacher-memory mechanism. Visual QA rejected both renders; binary publication itself is available.

analysis.tldr: AMD uses memory as training-free capability transfer: successful trajectories from a large teacher are distilled into workflow-, subtask-, and function-level memories whose retrieval timing is matched to the decision granularity of a small student agent.
analysis.problem: Small 4B–8B agents often cannot generate enough successful trajectories to bootstrap their own experience memory, while directly giving them teacher trajectories or one flat teacher-memory format can create a capability mismatch rather than usable guidance.
analysis.core_idea: Build three complementary memory views from successful teacher trajectories: Workflow memory abstracts task-level strategy, Subtask memory stores concrete intermediate behavioral examples, and Function memory captures tool-call conventions and pitfalls. Workflow and Subtask memories are retrieved proactively at task start; Function memory is retrieved reactively after tool-call errors.

memory_design.write: Offline, retain successful teacher trajectories and distill them into task-level workflows, semantically segmented subtask exemplars, and per-function examples/pitfalls.
memory_design.organize: Hierarchical procedural memory is aligned to three control granularities—task, subtask, and function—rather than one flat trajectory store.
memory_design.read: At task start, retrieve workflow guidance plus one example for each decomposed subtask; on a function-call error, retrieve the relevant function memory by function identity and inject it into the error context.
memory_design.update_forget: The evaluated student uses a teacher-built memory bank as a read-only transfer substrate; the paper does not study online student-side consolidation, deletion, or forgetting during evaluation.

compared_to: ReasoningBank adapted to the same teacher trajectories as a flat task-level memory baseline
MemP adapted to the same teacher trajectories as a procedural-memory baseline
SASM adapted to the same teacher trajectories as a uniform subtask-level memory baseline
analysis.evidence: Across Qwen3-4B, Gemma-4B-class, Qwen3-8B, and Llama3.1-8B students with GPT-5-mini as teacher, AMD reports average absolute gains over zero-shot of +27.2 percentage points on AppWorld, +11.2 on BFCL V3, and +3.4 on ToolSandbox, while outperforming the adapted memory baselines. The paper reports Subtask memory as the largest contributor and shows teacher usefulness depends on both teacher capability and student compatibility.
analysis.why_it_matters: The important design point is not merely hierarchical memory. It shows that memory can act as a non-parametric teacher→student transfer channel, but only when representation and retrieval timing are matched to what the weaker consumer can operationalize.
limitations: The gains are measured on three tool-use benchmarks with a strong external teacher; this is capability transfer, not evidence that small agents can self-evolve from their own sparse experience.
Teacher effectiveness depends on student compatibility as well as teacher strength, so a stronger teacher is not automatically a better memory source.
The evaluated memory bank is constructed offline from successful teacher trajectories; long-term online update, conflict, and forgetting are not studied.
The largest gains occur for weaker 4B students, so the value proposition may shrink as base-agent capability rises.
